sheet-1-1.description: Sheet 1 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the south-western corner of the Town of Irvington, at 100 feet to an inch. Most of the sheet is open ground. Olympic Park fills the upper left: its oval Half Mile Track runs across the sheet, with a theatre and a grand stand at the top left edge. 40th Street runs down the middle of the sheet to Stuyvesant Avenue, which enters from the top right, bends where Mill Road leaves it to the east, and continues south-west towards the Union County line; Harper Avenue meets Stuyvesant Avenue on the right. Webers Pond, a long narrow pond, lies at the top right, and its outlet brook runs south across the sheet beside 40th Street. Building is sparse: a few dwellings, sheds and a greenhouse at the top, and a cluster of dwellings, sheds and stables along Stuyvesant Avenue near the bend, where a fire alarm box and a hydrant stand. The Town Line with South Orange Township crosses the left half of the sheet as a dash-dot line and the Union County Line crosses the lower right corner. A framed inset at the left edge, drawn as a separate part, shows a further stretch of Stuyvesant Avenue at the town and county lines. Adjoining sheets are 2 above and 5 and 6 on the right.
notes: Olympic Park with its half-mile track and grand stand; the park is built over today.
Harper Av. is Harper Avenue in OpenStreetMap; the junction of 40th Street with Stuyvesant Avenue is today also the end of Boyden Avenue, which is not drawn.
Placed from three points along Stuyvesant Avenue (one hand-picked): an exact fit with no redundancy.

100 ft. South-west corner of Irvington: Olympic Park half-mile track, Webers Pond, Stuyvesant Avenue, 40th Street, Mill Road, Harper Avenue. Two parts: 1 main map (3 points on Stuyvesant, exact fit, low confidence); 2 framed inset at the left edge (Stuyvesant Avenue at the town and Union County lines), not placed.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Stuyvesant Avenue at the South Orange Township and Union County lines (no street junction drawn in the inset; needs an anchor where Stuyvesant Avenue crosses the county line, or parcel corners).

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the south-west part of Irvington at 100 feet to an inch, around the junction of Halstead Avenue and Prospect Avenue with the numbered cross streets. The streets run in two grids: 37th to 43rd Streets cross Halstead and Prospect Avenues in the upper right, while Olympic Terrace and Leslie Place run down the lower left to Stuyvesant Avenue along the bottom edge. Springfield Avenue cuts diagonally across the top right corner, where 44th Street ends in a narrow triangular wedge of lots by the Township Line. The blocks between 40th and 43rd Streets are laid out in narrow lots with scattered frame dwellings and sheds, and a few buildings stand along Halstead Avenue. At the upper left, outside the street grid, lie the grounds of Olympic Park, an amusement park with a dance hall and restaurant, a merry-go-round, a roller toboggan, booths, platforms and long sheds, and the edge of a circular track appears at the left margin. The park straddles the dashed line of the South Orange town line. Webers Pond lies at the lower left, drained by a stream that runs east across the sheet, passing under Halstead Avenue and the lower blocks. Lower blocks between 37th and 39th Streets are mostly empty lots. A small blacksmith shop is drawn in the 44th Street wedge, and a fire alarm box stands on Stuyvesant Avenue. Street widths of 50, 60, 70 and 86 feet are marked. Adjoining sheets are 1 on the left, 3 on the right, 4 above right and 6 below.
notes: Halstead Avenue is Chancellor Avenue in OpenStreetMap today.
37th Street has no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
The dashed Town Line and Township Line cross the sheet between Irvington and South Orange.
43rd Street / Prospect / Springfield and Prospect / Stuyvesant were measured 16 to 18 m from the fit and rejected; the modern junctions have moved.
100 ft. Prospect Av, 37th-44th Sts, Springfield Av, Halstead Av (now Chancellor Av), Olympic Ter, Leslie Pl.

sheet-3-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 3 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the south-western part of Irvington around Springfield Avenue, at 100 feet to an inch. On the left, Prospect Avenue runs down the sheet and is crossed by the short numbered streets 42nd, 41st, 40th, 39th, 38th and 37th, platted into narrow lots with only a few dwellings, mostly near 41st and 42nd streets; 43rd Street is lettered at the left edge. Springfield Avenue crosses the upper half of the sheet diagonally, with Headley Terrace, Florence Avenue, Elmwood Terrace and Sanford Avenue meeting it from the north. Along the south side of Springfield Avenue stand frame dwellings and stables and two long ranges of greenhouses, and Hose Company No. 4 of the volunteer fire service stands near 41st Street. A private drive leads in from Springfield Avenue. The lower right corner shows Durand Place and Wilson Place, lined with small dwellings, and Stuyvesant Avenue crosses the bottom of the sheet, where Yale Avenue meets it. Much of the middle of the sheet is open ground, numbered as large blocks. The upper right corner of the sheet holds a framed inset drawn at 50 feet to an inch, a separate part showing the William Kolle glue works by the Elizabeth River and Drakes Upper Pond (see sheet 19). Adjoining sheets are 2 on the left, 4 above, 14 and 8 on the right and 7 below.
notes: Hose Company No. 4 (volunteer service) on Springfield Avenue near 41st Street.
Two ranges of greenhouses south of Springfield Avenue.
37th Street has no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
The drawn junction of Headley Terrace with Springfield Avenue matches the modern node of 40th Street and Springfield Avenue within 2.5 m; the control point carries the modern name.

100 ft. Prospect Avenue, 37th to 42nd Streets, Springfield Avenue, Stuyvesant Avenue, Durand and Wilson Places. Two parts: 1 main map; 2 framed inset at top right at 50 ft (Kolle glue works, ice houses, Orange Place, Drakes Upper Pond; see sheet 19).

sheet-3-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 3 of the 1909 Newark volume five is the framed inset at the top right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned to its own angle with a north arrow pointing up and to the right. It shows the ground at the foot of Drakes Upper Pond in Irvington, where the Elizabeth River leaves the pond. A water-coloured band marks the river and the east shore of the pond, which curves down the right side; a narrow dam or spillway crosses the neck of the river at the top. The inset is lettered See Sheet No. 19 and is the same ground drawn on sheet 19. William Kolle Blue Works occupies the pink buildings at the left, described as a tank and press room, boiling room and mixing and drying room with a night watchman and no clock, steam heat and no lights, no pails, hose or chemical extinguishers. Southeast of it a large frame structure of two ice houses 22 feet to the eaves is drawn in yellow. At the lower left Orange Place runs diagonally across the inset, 40 feet wide, with a hydrant on it. The inset is bounded by a heavy line and carries its own scale note.
notes: Placed from the four corners of the ice houses carried from sheet 19, with the 50 ft scale and north taken from the fit; low confidence (one building, no street junction).
Fitted scale is about 1 percent below the nominal 50 ft scan constant.

100 ft. Prospect Avenue, 37th to 42nd Streets, Springfield Avenue, Stuyvesant Avenue, Durand and Wilson Places. Two parts: 1 main map; 2 framed inset at top right at 50 ft (Kolle glue works, ice houses, Orange Place, Drakes Upper Pond; see sheet 19).

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the western part of Irvington along Springfield Avenue and Elmwood Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the right. Springfield Avenue runs down the left side of the sheet; Elmwood Avenue runs parallel to it about 600 feet to the east. Headley Terrace, Franklin, Webster, Florence Avenue, Elmwood Terrace and Sanford Avenue cross between them, with Tiffany Place running down the right side. The South Orange town line crosses the upper part diagonally and the Township Line is lettered along it. The district is thinly built: a large undivided tract fills the upper middle of the sheet, and most blocks hold a few frame dwellings and stables on long narrow lots, with many lots empty. A public school, the Florence Avenue Public School, stands at Florence Avenue and Springfield Avenue, drawn in pink. A church and several buildings stand along the upper end of Springfield Avenue near Prospect Avenue, and a fire alarm box is marked on Springfield Avenue and on Elmwood Avenue at Florence Avenue. Street widths of 50 and 60 feet are marked. The edges of sheets 2 and 3 appear on the left, with the ends of Prospect Avenue and of 40th, 41st and 42nd Streets, and sheets 14 and 15 adjoin below and on the right.
notes: Franklin is Franklin Terrace in OpenStreetMap today; Webster is Webster Street.
The sheet is turned so that north points to the right (fitted rotation about 92 degrees).
The Township Line and Town Line are lettered along the dashed South Orange boundary.
100 ft, turned (north right). Springfield Av, Headley Ter, Elmwood, Florence, Sanford Avs, Franklin, Webster, Tiffany Pl.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the south-west corner of Irvington at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north points up and to the right. Stuyvesant Avenue forms the top edge. Below it a large platted tract is laid out between Mill Road on the left and Harper Avenue on the right, with Stewart Avenue and Lindsley Avenue running between them and crossed by Park Place near the top and Union Place near the bottom. Almost all of the tract consists of long rows of narrow empty lots; the only buildings are a few frame dwellings, shesheds and stables along Stuyvesant Avenue, where a milk depot stands, and a scatter of dwellings and chicken coops at the left and lower left. A dash-dot county line, lettered as the Union County line, runs down the left side of the sheet and meets Union Avenue and Elizabeth Road at a junction in the lower left. Across the bottom the Elizabeth River winds from left to right, and a side channel leads to Drakes Ice Pond with its ice house. Near the river stand the Old Irvington Mill, marked not operated, and the Union Avenue Hotel. Street widths of 50 feet are marked on most streets. Adjoining sheets are 1 above, 4 on the left, 6 on the right and 36 below.
notes: Elizabeth Road is not in OpenStreetMap today.
Park Place on this sheet has no matching modern junction; it was not used.
Stewart Avenue / Union Place was measured 11.6 m off by the detector (a narrow pair) and replaced by a hand-picked point.
Only five control points; the part is low confidence.
100 ft. Stuyvesant Av, Mill Road, Stewart, Lindsley, Harper Avs, Union Pl; few points nearly on one line (low-medium).

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the south part of Irvington below Stuyvesant Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that north points up and to the right. Stuyvesant Avenue crosses the top of the sheet from upper left to lower right, with Olympic Terrace, Leslie Place and Halstead Avenue running south from it and Prospect Avenue running down the right edge. Most of the sheet is open, undivided land: one very large tract fills the middle and left, with a few frame dwellings and shesheds along Stuyvesant Avenue and a single shed in the open field. The Elizabeth River crosses the lower part from left to right and widens into Drakes Lower Pond, marked as 94 feet above tide water, with an ice house on its western shore. A dam and drain are drawn at the left end. Below the river, at the lower left, stand the Scale Manufacturing works, which heat with stove and light with lamps, together with dwellings and coops on a narrow lane. Union Avenue runs along the bottom edge with Prospect Avenue meeting it at a fire alarm box. At the right edge, Nesbit Terrace, Park Place, Lincoln Place and Maple Place enter from sheet 7, and a group of dwellings and sheds stands near Nesbit Terrace. Street widths of 50, 60 and 70 feet are marked. Adjoining sheets are 1 and 2 above, 5 on the left, 7 on the right and 35 and 36 below.
notes: Halstead Avenue is Chancellor Avenue in OpenStreetMap today.
Prospect Avenue / Stuyvesant Avenue: the modern node lies about 47 m from the drawn junction and was left out.
Only three control points, all along Stuyvesant Avenue, so the part is a helmert and low confidence.
A narrow lane at the lower left, lettered Lane, is not named legibly.
100 ft. Stuyvesant Av (Olympic, Leslie, Chancellor), Prospect Av, Nesbit Ter; helmert on 3 points along Stuyvesant (low). Prospect/Stuyvesant node 47 m from the drawn junction.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows a large part of southern Irvington at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north points up and to the right. Stuyvesant Avenue crosses the top of the sheet diagonally, and Union Avenue runs along the bottom. Between them Yale Avenue runs from Stuyvesant Avenue towards Union Avenue, crossed by Nesbit Terrace, Park Place, Lincoln Place and Oak Place, while Maple Place and Elm Place run south from Lincoln Place at the left. Lyons Avenue and Prospect Avenue appear at the right and top edges. The blocks are a newly platted residential subdivision with long rows of narrow lots, almost all vacant; a few frame dwellings, coops and sheds stand along Stuyvesant Avenue and at the lower left. The Elizabeth River crosses the sheet from the left edge to the right, and a brook running south from it to Union Avenue is lettered on the right. Below the river a large tract is lettered Clinton Cemetery. At the right edge, near Union Avenue, a printing office with its own heat and light notation and a few dwellings are drawn. At the top left, a cluster of large buildings continues from the neighbouring sheet. Street widths of 50, 60 and 80 feet are marked. Adjoining sheets are 3 above, 6 on the left, 35 below and 10 and 11 on the right.
notes: Yale Avenue, Nesbit Terrace, Park Place, Lincoln Place, Maple Place, Elm Place and Oak Place all appear in OpenStreetMap with the same names.
Lyons Avenue junctions at the right edge lie 76 to 93 ft off the sheet and were not used.
The sheet is turned so that north points up and to the right (fitted rotation about 66 degrees).
100 ft. Stuyvesant to Union Av, Nesbit Ter, Park, Lincoln, Maple, Elm, Oak Pls, Yale Av; Elizabeth River, Clinton Cemetery.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 of the 1909 Newark volume five is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and shows the junction of Lyons Avenue, Stuyvesant Avenue and Springfield Avenue in the centre of Irvington. The sheet is turned so that north points to the right and slightly up. Springfield Avenue runs down the right side, an 85 foot street, with Elmwood Avenue entering from the right. Lyons Avenue crosses from the lower left to Springfield Avenue at the top, meeting Wilson Place, which runs from the upper left, and Stuyvesant Avenue, which branches to the lower right towards Springfield Avenue. Stuyvesant Place runs parallel below, continuing Nesbit Terrace from sheet 7, and Durand Place curves in at the top. The blocks hold a mixture of vacant lots and scattered frame dwellings, with a row of factory or workshop buildings at the top near Durand Place and Springfield Avenue. The Colored Home for Aged and Orphans of New Jersey stands near the bottom right, between Stuyvesant Avenue and Stuyvesant Place. A fire alarm box marks Stuyvesant Avenue at the right edge, and a bridge-like jog marks the end of Elmwood Avenue near sheet 14. Street widths of 50, 60, 80 and 85 feet are marked, and the scale bar reads in feet. Adjoining sheets are 3 above, 7 on the left, 9 below and 14 on the right.
notes: Stuyvesant Place on this sheet continues Nesbit Terrace and is part of modern Nesbit Terrace.
Fitted from only two junctions (Lyons / Nesbit Terrace and Lyons / Springfield) with a helmert: low confidence.
Lyons Avenue / Wilson Place and Lyons Avenue / Stuyvesant Avenue are 9 to 10 m from a fit through the other points, so Lyons Avenue's modern junctions here may be displaced; both were left out.

50 ft, turned. Lyons, Stuyvesant and Springfield Avs, Wilson and Durand Pls, Stuyvesant Pl (now Nesbit Ter); Colored Home for Aged and Orphans. Anchored on 2 points (low); Lyons Av junctions 9-10 m off.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the western part of the Town of Irvington at 50 feet to an inch, a district of frame dwellings on narrow lots. The sheet is turned so that streets run diagonally across the page. Springfield Avenue and Park Avenue cross the upper left, and Park Place runs down the middle of the sheet to Weber Place, where it meets a block bounded on the east by Lincoln Place. Lincoln Place forms the eastern edge of the built-up area and curves toward Lyons Avenue at the bottom right corner. Most lots carry two and two and a half storey dwellings with outbuildings; the Deutsch Evangelische Gemeinde Kirche stands at the head of the block between Park Avenue and Lincoln Place, and the large Bethanien Altenheim (an old people's home, with its own steam heating and lighting note) occupies a ground at the left edge between Park Place and Stuyvesant Place. A fire alarm box and several dwellings with hydrants line Park Place. The lower third is largely open ground and long unbuilt lots, with a fan of narrow lots along the bottom edge belonging to another block. A compass rose drawn in the upper right shows north pointing up and to the left. Adjoining sheets are numbered 11 and 12 above, 14 and 8 to the left, 10 to the right and 7 below.
notes: Park Avenue on this sheet is today's Nye Avenue; the drawn Park Place, Weber Place, Lincoln Place and Lyons Avenue keep their names.
Stuyvesant Place at the left edge is not in the modern street network under that name; its lettering is split across two segments of the street, so the reading is medium confidence.
Bethanien Altenheim is the large institution at the left edge; Deutsch Evangelische Gemeinde Kirche stands near the top of the block between Park Avenue and Lincoln Place.
Georeferenced from six detected junctions (Lincoln, Weber, Park Place, Nye and Lyons), RMSE about 1.3 m; the sheet is rotated about 43 degrees from the other Irvington sheets.
50 ft. Springfield Av, Park Av (now Nye Av), Weber, Lincoln, Stuyvesant Pls, Lyons Av.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the southern part of Irvington between Lincoln Place on the west and Union Avenue on the east, at 50 feet to an inch. Park Avenue crosses the top left corner and Lyons Avenue closes the sheet at the bottom. The Elizabeth River winds from the top left to the bottom of the sheet, drawn in blue with its banks. The sheet is mostly a long strip of deep lots running back from the two avenues, many of them still open. Dwellings line Lincoln Place on the left, with a pink brick building among them near Weber Place, and along Union Avenue on the right. In the middle of the sheet lie long narrow greenhouses labelled Green Ho. in the upper and lower parts, together with barns and sheds along the river bank. A fire alarm box stands at Union Avenue and Lyons Avenue. The sheet is turned so that streets run on a diagonal, with a compass rose at the left edge. Adjoining sheets are 12 above, 9 on the left, 7 below and 33 and 34 on the right.
notes: Park Avenue is today's Nye Avenue.
The long structures labelled Green Ho. are greenhouses; the reading of the small lettering on them is low confidence.

Georeferenced from four junctions (Lincoln/Weber, Lincoln/Lyons, Lyons/Union, Lincoln/Nye), RMSE 0.9 m. The Lincoln/Lyons point was measured about 29 ft from where the street centreline appears to fall on the sheet; it is medium confidence.
50 ft. Park Av (Nye Av), Lincoln Pl, Union and Lyons Avs, Weber Pl; Elizabeth River. 4 points.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the centre of Irvington at 50 feet to an inch. Drakes Pond, drawn in blue with a note giving its level as 122 feet above tide water, fills the left half of the sheet, with its outlet stream running south under Springfield Avenue. Clinton Avenue crosses the top and Springfield Avenue the bottom; between them run Smith Street and Orange Avenue on the right and, at the top, Drakes Lane. East of Smith Street the blocks are filled with dwellings on narrow lots, with a group of larger outbuildings and sheds in the lower right corner, two of them coloured green. A mill or factory with a long narrow raceway stands at the upper end of the pond beside Clinton Avenue, and a large ice house stands at the left edge of the sheet west of the pond. Along Lake Street at the bottom left stand works with attached sheds. A compass rose in the pond area gives north. Adjoining sheets are 19 above, 14 to the left, 12 to the right and below, and 9 at the bottom left.
notes: The lettering on the works at the upper end of the pond and on the ice house is small; the names of firms were not read and are left out.
Smith Street is lettered only as Smith along the main block and North Smith Street at the top.
Georeferenced from six junctions, RMSE 1.1 m, leave-one-out 2.5 m, 7.59 px/ft.
50 ft. Clinton Av, Smith St, Orange and Springfield Avs, Lake, Drakes Lane; Drakes Pond.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the business centre of Irvington around Springfield Avenue, at 50 feet to an inch. Springfield Avenue runs diagonally from the lower left to the upper right, lined with stores, a post office near the top, a bakery, a feed store, a laundry and a wagon shed. Park Avenue runs parallel below it, with dwellings on long lots, and New runs across both between them. Orange Avenue enters from the upper left and Clinton Avenue crosses the top, with a row of dwellings along its south side and the Irvington Hotel at the upper right. Churches stand along the sheet: the First Reformed Church with its gymnasium and club room, and the Irvington Methodist Episcopal Church near Union Avenue, which closes the sheet on the right. The Elizabeth River crosses the lower left corner. Pink fill marks the brick stores along Springfield Avenue; a green building near the Methodist church is a small shop. A compass rose at the left shows north. Adjoining sheets are 21 and 27 above, 11 to the left, 31 and 34 to the right and 10 below.
notes: Park Avenue is today's Nye Avenue.
Union Avenue is printed in two parts along the street (Union and Av.), read as Union Avenue.
Streets here are drawn wider than the modern right-of-way (Springfield Avenue about 100 ft against 85 ft); the junctions carry residuals of 3 to 5 m.
Georeferenced from only four detected junctions, RMSE 2.2 m, no leave-one-out possible: low confidence.

50 ft. Springfield Av business centre, Orange Av, New, Park Av (Nye Av), Union Av. 4 points, scale -3.5 percent; low. Offset Cummings/New crossing at Clinton Av gives a 9 m shared-junction misfit with 21-1.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows an industrial district of Irvington next to the Newark city line, at 50 feet to an inch. Cottage Street runs across the top of the sheet, and three streets run down from it: South Grove on the left, Coit in the middle and Woolsey on the right, with a siding or track drawn along Woolsey. The blocks between them are given over to factories, drawn in detail with their rooms, power plants and fire protection. Between Coit and Woolsey stand the Eastern Cut Sole Company tannery (milling, tan yard, beam house and warehouse), the novelty works of Jos. Ross Jr. and Company, and further down the Irvington Manufacturing Company, makers of drop forged tools. East of Woolsey lies the Glorieux Smelting and Refining Works, a long range of furnace, refining and crystallizing rooms with a copper yard. Between South Grove and Coit is the Richard Best lead pencil factory, and a row of small buildings lines South Grove at the left edge. Much of the lower half of the sheet is still open ground, divided into blocks 5, 6 and 7. A north arrow and the scale of feet are drawn at the right and bottom. Adjoining sheets are 42 above, 40 on the left and 41 on the right and below.
notes: Cottage (Street) is today part of Nye Avenue; South Grove is Grove Street; Woolsey north of Lyons Avenue no longer exists as a named street.
Factories: Eastern Cut Sole Co. tannery, Glorieux Smelting and Refining Works, Richard Best lead pencil factory, Jos. Ross Jr. and Co. novelty works, The Irvington Mfg. Co. (drop forged tools).
Placed from the two junctions on Cottage Street (77 m apart): anchored at the atlas scale with rotation from the drawn street lines.

50 ft. Factory district: Cottage (now Nye Avenue), South Grove, Coit, Woolsey; Eastern Cut Sole tannery, Glorieux smelting works, Best pencil factory. Anchored on Cottage/Coit (two junctions 77 m apart), low confidence.

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows an outlying part of Irvington at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north points to the right of the page. Stuyvesant Avenue crosses the lower third from Springfield Avenue at the left to Clinton Avenue West at the right. Laurel Avenue runs down the middle of the sheet and Sanford Avenue along the top. In the upper left, Chapman Place and Elmwood Avenue meet in a block of small dwellings on narrow lots, with a fan of lots drawn where Elmwood Avenue and Springfield Avenue diverge. A block of lots between Sherman Place, Grant Place and Clinton Avenue West at the right has a row of dwellings along Clinton. Tremont and Lake streets cross the lower part, where dwellings and a larger works with shops line Stuyvesant Avenue near Springfield. Large parts of the middle of the sheet, blocks 4 and 6, are open ground. A compass rose at the top right shows north pointing right. Adjoining sheets are 4 and 3 above, 8 and 9 to the left, 15 above right, 17 to the right and 11 below.
notes: Park Avenue is today's Nye Avenue. Clinton Avenue West is printed Clinton Av. W. and is today part of Clinton Avenue.
Georeferenced from ten junctions, RMSE 1.2 m, leave-one-out 1.7 m, 3.80 px/ft; the sheet is rotated about 88 degrees.
Rejected as realigned: Chapman Place / Springfield Avenue (14 m) and Clinton Avenue / Grant Place (11 m).
100 ft, turned (north right). Sanford, Chapman, Elmwood, Laurel, Stuyvesant, Grant, Sherman, Newton, Clinton Av W.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 of the 1909 Newark volume five is a sparsely built sheet along the line between the City of Newark and the Town of Irvington, at 100 feet to an inch. Clinton Avenue crosses the middle from the lower left to the right, meeting Sanford Avenue, which runs down the right side. North of Clinton Avenue is a large tract cut into long narrow lots on either side of Ridgewood Avenue, marked as not opened, with a handful of dwellings near Sanford Avenue. The town line between Newark and Irvington is drawn as a dash and dot line running diagonally across the sheet from lower left to upper right, with the South Orange township boundary running down the left edge. The large middle block 8 is open ground. Along the bottom edge is a row of dwellings on narrow lots on Tiffany Place, crossed by Franklin Street, Webster Street and Florence Avenue, and a strip of lots continues along Sanford Avenue near the bottom right. A compass rose at the lower left shows north pointing up and slightly left. Adjoining sheets are 16 above, 17 to the right, 14 below right and 4 below.
notes: Ridgewood Avenue is lettered Not Opened on this sheet; its modern line is about 80 ft from the drawn one and it was left out of the street list.
Placed by a single measured junction (Clinton Avenue / Sanford Avenue) with the scale of sheet 14 and north taken from the street lines; low confidence.
The boundary lettering along the town line was read at overview scale only and is medium confidence.
100 ft. Newark/Irvington line; Clinton and Sanford Avs, Ridgewood (not opened). Anchored on Clinton/Sanford (low).

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the western edge of Irvington along the South Orange Township line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Sanford Avenue runs down the right side of the sheet, bending slightly to the south-west, and the only built-up streets lie east of a block of long narrow lots between it and Cumberland Street: Ivy, Netherwood Place, Mount Vernon Place, Mountain View Place and Fleetwood Place cross from Cumberland to Sanford Avenue at intervals of about 250 feet. The blocks are numbered 4130 to 4135 and the lots are laid out in long rows, but only a handful of frame dwellings, sheds and stables stand on them, so the district was newly platted and almost empty. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches are dotted along Netherwood, Mountain View and Fleetwood Places and Sanford Avenue. The upper two thirds of the sheet is blank apart from block and tract numbers (4127, 4148, 4136) and a few property lines, and the whole left side is left to the South Orange Township boundary, lettered along a dashed line. Near the bottom a few frame dwellings and sheds stand on the large tract 4136 beside the Town of Irvington line, which crosses the lower right corner at an angle. A compass rose and the scale bar are printed at left and bottom left. Adjoining sheets are 23 above, 18 and 17 to the east and 15 below.
notes: Sanford Avenue is placed from five junctions along one street, so the part is a two-parameter fit along that line (low confidence across the street direction).
Cumberland is not in OpenStreetMap under that name; the nearest modern street, Ellery Avenue, lies about 45 m east of where the sheet draws it and was left out of the control.
Mountain View Place is Mountainview Place in OpenStreetMap; Mount Vernon Place meets Sanford Avenue at a node also named Mt Vernon Place East.
100 ft. Sanford Av, Ivy, Netherwood, Mt Vernon, Mountain View, Fleetwood Pls, Cumberland; mostly vacant. Helmert on Sanford only (low).

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 of the 1909 Newark volume five lies along the Newark and Irvington boundary and is drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Sanford Avenue forms the left edge, running south-west from Mountain View Place to West Clinton Avenue at the bottom; Stuyvesant Avenue is the straight right-hand street. Between them lie two blocks of narrow lots (4087 to 4089) opening on Summit Avenue and Hillside Avenue, which run down from Mountain View Place, and a diagonal dash-dot line marks the Town of Irvington boundary across the upper half. Mountain View Place and Fleetwood Place cross the district from Sanford Avenue to Stuyvesant Avenue, with Netherwood Place and Mount Vernon Place appearing as stubs at the top left and Madison Avenue lettered across Stuyvesant Avenue at the top right. A large open tract (4083) at the top right holds a few sheds and dwellings. The middle of the sheet, below Fleetwood Place and between Sanford and Stuyvesant Avenues, is mostly blank land; frame dwellings and outbuildings cluster along Stuyvesant Avenue and Newton Place, and the lower blocks (numbered 1 and 2) have long lots running back from Stuyvesant Avenue. At the bottom West Clinton Avenue crosses the sheet, with Sherman Place, Newton Place and Grant Place leaving it. A fire alarm box stands at Stuyvesant and Clinton. Adjoining sheets are 16 to the left, 15 at lower left, 18 above, 19 and 20 to the right and 14 below.
notes: Hillside Avenue is now Hillside Terrace in OpenStreetMap; Summit Avenue and the drawn Fleetwood Place east of Sanford Avenue no longer exist.
West Clinton Avenue is Clinton Avenue today.
Mountain View Place is Mountainview Place in OpenStreetMap.
100 ft. Sanford to Stuyvesant, Mountain View Pl to Clinton Av W; 3 hand-picked points.

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers north-western Irvington between Lindsley Avenue and the Newark line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Sanford Avenue runs down the left edge and Stuyvesant Avenue forms the straight eastern boundary of the main blocks; Smith, Mead and Brookdale run north and south between them, and Norwood lies in the upper right. Ocean Avenue, Commonwealth Avenue and Lexington Avenue cross east and west, with blocks 4099 to 4109 laid out in long rows of narrow lots in between. Short places (Noll, Helen, Florence and Cliff Hill) leave Sanford Avenue at the upper left. Most lots are vacant; frame dwellings stand at intervals, chiefly along Sanford and Stuyvesant Avenues and on the north side of Lexington Avenue. At the upper right Valley, Lindsley and Brookdale cross a more irregular set of blocks (4073 and 4074) where Stuyvesant Avenue changes direction. The southern half of the sheet is open land in large tracts (4099, 4100) with a few houses and outbuildings, crossed by a dashed Town of Irvington boundary near the foot of Stuyvesant Avenue, with Ivy Street, Summit Avenue and Hillside Avenue ending at the bottom. A pink building and several farm buildings stand in the central tract. Adjoining sheets are 23, 16 and 17 to the west and south, 24 above, 25 to the north-east and 20 to the east.
notes: Ocean Avenue is now 18th Avenue and Lexington Avenue is now Lenox Street in OpenStreetMap (matched by spacing and detected junctions).
Valley is Valley Street and Norwood is Norwood Street today; the Stuyvesant Avenue / Valley Street junction was 7 to 8 m off and was rejected.

Summit Avenue no longer exists and Hillside Avenue is Hillside Terrace; Cliff Hill Place and the Noll, Helen and Florence Places carry residuals of 2 to 3 m because their modern lines differ from the drawn ones.
100 ft. Sanford, Smith, Mead, Stuyvesant, Lindsley to Ivy, Ocean Av (18th Av), Lexington Av (Lenox St).

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows central Irvington between Stuyvesant Avenue on the left and Orange Avenue on the right, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. The Elizabeth River winds from the top across the sheet to the bottom and widens into Drakes Upper Pond, lettered 136 feet above tide water, in the middle. East of the pond Lenox Avenue runs diagonally and Allyn, Madison Avenue, Wilson, Rich and Orange Place cross it, enclosing numbered blocks (1 to 6) of long narrow lots with frame dwellings, coops and sheds. In block 4 stand the Denman Glass Bending Works and the Swiss Weaving Works. At the foot of the pond a small inset area marked See Sheet No. 3 shows the ice houses and the William Kolle blue works. Further south Drakes Lane and North Smith run between small groups of dwellings, and Clinton Avenue West closes the sheet at the bottom, with South Smith Street and Orange Avenue leaving it to the south. West of the pond the large tracts between Stuyvesant Avenue and the river are mostly open, with scattered houses and farm buildings along Stuyvesant Avenue, and Mountain View Place and Fleetwood Place enter from the left edge. A dashed Madison Avenue is drawn across the north-west tract. The area around the sheet number is left to adjoining sheets 17, 18, 20, 21, 11 and 14.
notes: Allyn is Allen Street and Wilson is Oakland Street in OpenStreetMap; Rich is Rich Street; North Smith and South Smith are Smith Street.
The dashed Madison Avenue west of Lenox Avenue is a projected street; its junction with Stuyvesant Avenue was left out of the fit (3.3 m residual).
Block 5 carries a See Sheet No. 3 reference to the inset on sheet 3 (part 2).
100 ft. Lenox and Orange Avs, Madison, Wilson, Rich, Allyn; Drakes Upper Pond, Elizabeth River.

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers Irvington from the Newark line near Stuyvesant Avenue east to Orange Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. The Elizabeth River enters at the centre and leaves at the bottom beside Lenox Avenue, which runs diagonally north-east. East of it Kosciusko, Caserta, Sorrento, Allyn and Madison Avenue cross to Orange Avenue, enclosing numbered blocks 1 to 4 of long narrow lots; a row of lettered frame dwellings stands on block 3. At the top Valley runs south-east from Stuyvesant Avenue to Orange Avenue, passing Brookdale Avenue, Sun Set Avenue, Alexander and West End Avenue, which run north into the blocks 4073A and 4075A of narrow lots. Ocean Avenue and Norwood Street end at the top edge. The Town of Irvington line cuts a long dashed diagonal across the large open tract 4076, which fills the western half of the sheet; only a few sheds and a dwelling stand on it, near Stuyvesant Avenue. Stuyvesant Avenue forms the left edge, and Commonwealth Avenue, Lexington Avenue and Lane appear as stubs of the neighbouring sheet 18. Hydrants, water pipes and fire alarm boxes are marked along the streets. Adjoining sheets are 18, 25, 22, 21 and 19.
notes: Kosciusko is Bachman Place, Caserta is Bamford Place and Sorrento is Adams Street in OpenStreetMap; Allyn is Allen Street.
Ocean Avenue is 18th Avenue and Lexington Avenue is Lenox Street today; Sun Set Avenue is Sunset Avenue.
The Brookdale Avenue / Valley Street (4.2 m) and Madison Avenue / Stuyvesant Avenue (3.7 m) junctions were left out of the fit; Stuyvesant Avenue / Valley Street was rejected at 7.8 m.
100 ft. Orange Av to Stuyvesant, Lenox, Valley, Kosciusko (Bachman Pl), Caserta (Bamford Pl), Sorrento (Adams St).

sheet-21-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 21 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers central Irvington between Orange Avenue on the left and Myrtle Avenue on the right, from Woodlawn Place at the top to Clinton Avenue West at the bottom, at 100 feet to an inch. Orange Avenue runs down the left edge with a continuous row of frame dwellings on its east side; the ends of Sorrento, Allyn, Madison, Wilson, Rich and Orange Place streets of the next sheet are lettered beyond it. Cummings Street runs parallel to it and is also lined with dwellings. Linden Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally from the bottom to the top right. The upper right block between Linden and Myrtle avenues is laid out in small lots along Woodlawn Place, Fuller Place, Avon Avenue, Garwood Place and Madison Avenue, with modest frame houses. The middle of the sheet is largely open: a large lot with the greenhouses and potting sheds of E. W. Fengar, florist, beside Linden Avenue, and empty blocks along Madison Avenue, Ruth, Stanley and Bell, with Irvington Place leading off on the right. A framed inset at the lower right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and treated as a separate part, shows the Irvington Varnish and Insulator Company between Tremont Terrace and Argyle Terrace (the area of sheet 48). Adjoining sheets are 20 and 19 on the left, 22 above, 47 on the right and 27 and 28 below.
notes: E. W. Fengar, florist: greenhouses by Linden Avenue.
Irvington Place has no named way in OpenStreetMap today; Allyn Street and Sorrento Street are not in OpenStreetMap either.
Fuller Place / Linden Avenue is drawn about 10 m from the modern junction and was not used.
The Madison Avenue / Myrtle Avenue junction was measured from a wrong line pair and left out.

100 ft. Orange Avenue to Myrtle Avenue, Woodlawn Place to Clinton Avenue West. Two parts: 1 main map; 2 framed inset at bottom right at 50 ft (Irvington Varnish and Insulator Co., Tremont and Argyle Terraces; area of sheet 48).

sheet-21-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 21 of the 1909 Newark volume five is a framed inset at the lower right of the sheet, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that Tremont Terrace runs along the top and Argyle Terrace along the bottom. It shows the works of the Irvington Varnish and Insulator Company between the two terraces, the same ground as sheet 48 on the main series. The principal building, drawn in yellow with brick (pink) additions, holds the dressing, motor, winding, cloth machine, shipping and grinding rooms and the office; a further pink block holds the cloth machine room and the engine, with a chimney 70 feet high, and a narrow open coal bin runs to the right towards a small separate building. At the far right stand the boiler room, a storage room and a varnish storage room with patent stone. The firm's note reads one watchman, no clock, light electricity, heat steam, power steam and fuel coal. The lots of the two terraces, drawn as a regular fringe of narrow parcels, are empty. The block number 14 and the scale note 50 ft to an inch are printed. The inset is separated from the main map by a heavy frame, and the main map of this sheet is part 1.
notes: Placed from five building corners carried from sheet 48, where the same works is drawn at 100 feet to an inch (low confidence: the buildings are small, and the inset is rotated about 9 degrees against sheet 48's drawing).

100 ft. Orange Avenue to Myrtle Avenue, Woodlawn Place to Clinton Avenue West. Two parts: 1 main map; 2 framed inset at bottom right at 50 ft (Irvington Varnish and Insulator Co., Tremont and Argyle Terraces; area of sheet 48).

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers a mostly undeveloped stretch on the Newark and Irvington boundary, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. At upper left the sheet is largely blank paper crossed by Orange Avenue, which runs up from the left edge to the five-way meeting with Valley Street, Alexander Street and West End Avenue; a dash-dot line along the town boundary and a compass rose lie in the blank area. From that meeting Valley Street runs up to Sun Set Avenue, and the blocks east of it (numbered 4050 and 4051) are platted into narrow lots between Sun Set Avenue, Alexander Street and West End Avenue as far as Ocean Avenue, but nothing is built there and several streets are lettered as not opened. Carolina Avenue and the blocks lettered 4043 and 4043A lie farther down, east of the boundary line, and below them Melrose, Arlington and Isabella avenues are laid out as long rows of empty lots between Halsey Place and Breakenridge. At the right edge the ends of Columbia Avenue and Munn Avenue are marked. A small group of buildings, with sheds and a storage yard, stands beside Orange Avenue at the left. At lower left the sheet shows a block of Linden Avenue between Woodlawn Place and Silkmen Place, with a few dwellings and coops; its lower edge is Myrtle Avenue, where Delmar Place and Tremont Terrace begin, and the corner numbers of neighbouring sheets 21, 47 and 48 are printed there. A Library of Congress map division stamp and a scale bar appear in the blank paper. Adjoining sheets are 20 above, 25 on the right, 21 on the left and 47 and 48 below.
notes: Sun Set Avenue is Sunset Avenue and Silkmen Place is Silkman Place in OpenStreetMap.

Alexander, Ocean Avenue, Carolina, Melrose, Arlington, Isabella and Halsey are partly lettered not opened; Ocean Avenue, Halsey Place, Arlington Avenue, Caserta Street and Kosciusko Street have no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
The five-way meeting of Orange Avenue, Valley Street, Alexander Street and West End Avenue is the one OpenStreetMap node.
The street names Delmar Place and Tremont Terrace are only partly legible at the lower edge, where they belong to sheet 48.
Georeferenced from only six junctions (the five-way and Sunset/Valley at the top, four at the lower left); the blocks at the right edge, 4000 to 6000 px from them, rest on extrapolation.
100 ft. Orange Av / Valley St five-way; unbuilt platted lots (Alexander, West End, Carolina, Melrose, Arlington, Isabella); Linden / Silkmen Pl block. Low-medium (right side uncontrolled).

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the Vailsburg district at the western edge of Newark, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. South Orange Avenue crosses the top of the sheet on a diagonal, with the area north of it left blank and lettered Volume Three; the city line between Newark and South Orange runs down the left side. The blocks below the avenue (numbered 4172 to 4179) are divided by Montrose, Dover, Saint Paul Avenue, Oakland Terrace, Richelieu Terrace and, at the right, Hazelwood Avenue, with Cliff Street crossing them midway and Fortuna Street crossing the upper right blocks. Dwellings along St. Paul Avenue and the streets east of it are built up with frame houses, outbuildings and stables, while the west end of the sheet is mostly empty lots. Notable buildings are the Vailsburg M. E. Church at the top right, the T. J. Rhinhardt machine shop on Oakland Terrace, and the Lincoln School, shaded as a brick building with heating and lighting noted, near the middle. In the lower right the platted streets turn to run north-east and south-west: Noll Place, Helen Place, Florence Place and Cliff Hill Place cross Sanford Avenue and Geneva, with Commonwealth Avenue and Lexington Avenue at the foot. The lower left of the sheet is blank apart from block numbers 4125 and 4125A, the neighbouring sheet numbers 16 and 18, a scale bar and library stamps. Water pipes with their sizes, hydrants and a fire alarm box are marked along the streets. Adjoining sheets are 24 on the east, 18 and 16 below and Volume Three above.
notes: Richelieu Terrace is the modern name for the street lettered Geneva south of Florence Place.
Geneva has no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
Saint Paul Avenue is St Paul Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The first letters of Commonwealth Avenue are hard to read on the scan; the reading follows the modern street name.
The areas north of South Orange Avenue and at the lower left are blank; Volume Three is lettered across the top.

Cliff Hill Place and Florence Place meet Sanford Avenue where the street bends; Florence Place / Sanford Avenue and Cliff Hill Place / Sanford Avenue were measured but rejected as 12 and 24 m off the fit.
100 ft. Vailsburg: South Orange Av to Cliff Hill Pl, Montrose to Hazelwood; Volume Three blank at top.

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the Vailsburg and north Irvington blocks between South Orange Avenue at the top and Lindsley Avenue at the bottom, from Hazelwood Avenue on the west to Brookdale Avenue on the east, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. The streets run roughly north to south (Hazelwood, Sanford, Smith, Mead, Salem, Stuyvesant, Norwood and Brookdale) and are crossed by short east-west streets: Rock, Fortuna, Abinger, Silver and Cliff, with Noll Place, Helen Place and Florence Place ending at Sanford Avenue on the lower left. The district is a newly platted residential suburb: long rows of narrow lots, many still empty, with scattered frame dwellings, coops, sheds and stables, and denser building along South Orange Avenue and Sanford Avenue. Along South Orange Avenue stand a row of stores and dwellings, the Kilburn Memorial Presbyterian Church with its school room, and a florist's greenhouse (C. Wonfor) on Salem Street. Water pipes with their sizes, hydrants and a fire alarm box are marked along the streets. The area above South Orange Avenue, lettered City of East Orange and Volume Three, is left blank apart from the ends of Palm, Sanford, Smith and Halstead streets, and the City Line is marked there. Block numbers in the 4100s and 4060s are printed in the blocks. Adjoining sheets are 23 on the west, 26 and 25 on the east and 18 below.
notes: Rock (between Smith and Stuyvesant) has no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
Abinger is Abinger Place in OpenStreetMap.
Volume Three is lettered across the blank area north of South Orange Avenue.
100 ft (pilot). Vailsburg / north Irvington: South Orange Avenue to Lindsley Avenue, Hazelwood to Brookdale Avenues. Blank Volume Three area above South Orange Avenue masked out.

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the Newark and Irvington boundary district between Brookdale Avenue at the top and Munn Avenue at the bottom, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. The long east-west streets (Brookdale, Boylan, Sunset, Alexander, West End and Carolina avenues, then Melrose, Vermont, Isabella and Columbia avenues, with Munn and South Munn avenues at the foot) run on a slight slant across the sheet, and the cross streets (Ocean Avenue, Spencer, Lindsley Avenue, Park Place, Laurel Place and Plymouth) are laid out between them. A dash-dot line lettered as the line between the City of Newark and the Town of Irvington crosses the lower left on a diagonal, with a compass rose near the middle. Almost all of the sheet is platted and unbuilt: block after block of narrow lots (numbered 4032 to 4075) with no buildings, and some streets such as Spencer and Grove Terrace marked 50 feet wide. Frame dwellings stand only in a few places, along Sunset and Alexander avenues in the upper right, on the north side of Carolina Avenue and Laurel Place, and in a row on Vermont Avenue beside Plymouth at the right edge. Water mains with their sizes and hydrants are shown along the open streets. Abinger Place begins at the top right edge. The corners carry the numbers of the neighbouring sheets, 18 and 24 above, 22 on the left, 26 on the right and 48 and 49 below, and a scale bar and library stamps appear at the bottom.
notes: South Munn Avenue is the same name in OpenStreetMap.
Plymouth is Plymouth Street in OpenStreetMap, but its modern line lies 4 to 7 m from the drawn one and it was left out of the fit.
Ocean, Arlington Avenue and Breakenridge Terrace at the left edge have no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
The line between the City of Newark and the Town of Irvington is lettered along the diagonal dash-dot line.
100 ft. Brookdale to Munn Av, Ocean Av to Plymouth; Plymouth St left out (displaced, narrow).

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the south-west corner of Irvington where it meets the Newark and East Orange line, from Brookdale Avenue at the top to South Munn Avenue at the bottom, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. South Orange Avenue runs down the right side on a long slant, and the blocks between it and Plymouth are closely built with frame dwellings, many of them two and a half storeys, along Boylan, Sunset, Alexander, West End, Vermont, Isabella and Columbia avenues. Sunset and Alexander avenues carry the heaviest building, including the Alexander Street School shaded as a brick building with stores and houses facing it, a Lutheran church and rows of small houses in the upper right near South Orange Avenue; a bowling alley and several stores stand at the north end near Brookdale Avenue, where a small stream crosses the top of the sheet in a blue line. Ricord, Howell Place, Plymouth and the lower end of Laurel Place cross the middle blocks, which are numbered 4031 to 4063. The right edge beyond South Orange Avenue is the city line of East Orange, lettered City Line, with Grand Avenue, Chelsea Avenue and North Munn Avenue entering from that side and a compass rose in the blank paper; Volume Three is lettered along the margin. Water pipes with sizes, hydrants, fire alarm boxes and lot numbers are marked throughout. Adjoining sheets are 25 on the west, 24 above and 49 and 50 below, and a Library of Congress stamp and scale bar are at the lower left.
notes: South Munn Avenue is the same name in OpenStreetMap; North Munn Avenue is on the East Orange side.
Plymouth is Plymouth Street in OpenStreetMap; its modern line is displaced 4 to 7 m from the drawn one and it was left out of the fit.
Ricord is Ricord Street in OpenStreetMap; Alexander and Boylan are Alexander Street and Boylan Street.
The label Chelsea Avenue is read from a hand-drawn A and could be read Chelser.
The area east of South Orange Avenue is lettered City of East Orange and belongs to Volume Three.
100 ft. Brookdale to South Munn Av, Plymouth to South Orange Av; East Orange blank; top uncontrolled.

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the centre of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Three east-west streets cross the sheet: Cummings at the top, Linden Avenue in the middle and Myrtle Avenue lower down, with Skinkle Lane and Washington at the foot. At the left edge Clinton Avenue curves down the side of the sheet, and Springfield Avenue, drawn 85 feet wide, cuts across the lower left corner on a diagonal. The principal public buildings stand in the left half: Irvington Public School No. 1, a large brick building with its fire-fighting equipment listed beside it, and the Town Hall with the Fire Department House No. 1 and a clock tower, whose notes list the apparatus and the men kept there. Below them a block of saloons, stores and a machine shop with a gas engine, an oven and fire rails fills the corner of Clinton and Springfield avenues, and Springfield Avenue is lined with a bowling alley, a coal yard, a saloon and an office. On Myrtle Avenue stand Trinity Episcopal Church with its Sunday School room, a stable and wagon shed, and rows of dwellings; plumbers' supplies and further frame houses front Linden Avenue. Houses are numbered along each street and lots are narrow, with most dwellings two and a half storeys in frame. The right half of the sheet is residential, with houses along the street fronts and open rear lots. A compass rose and a scale of feet are at the lower left. Adjoining sheets are 21 above, 28 on the right, 12 and 31 on the left and 29 below.
notes: Cummings is Cummings Street and Washington is Washington Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Skinkle Lane has no named way in OpenStreetMap today.
Clinton Avenue West and Clinton Avenue are both lettered along the left edge; the curve of the street there is only partly the modern Clinton Avenue.
The modern Myrtle Avenue / Springfield Avenue and Springfield Avenue / Washington Avenue nodes lie 15 to 20 m from the drawn junctions, so Springfield Avenue was not used for control.
Georeferenced from two junctions on Clinton Avenue, so the part is a two-point helmert and low confidence; the scale (7.48 px/ft) and rotation (58.5 degrees) agree with sheet 28.
50 ft. Irvington centre: Cummings, Linden, Myrtle, Washington, Clinton Av, Springfield Av. Helmert on 2 points (low); Springfield Av 15-20 m off and left out.

sheet-28.description: Sheet 28 of the 1909 Newark volume five continues the centre of Irvington east of sheet 27, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Cummings runs diagonally across the top, Linden Avenue and Myrtle Avenue cross the middle, and Skinkle Lane and Washington Avenue lie along the bottom, with Bell, Stanley and Ruth running north and south between Cummings and Linden Avenue and Madison Avenue marking the east side, where its northern end is lettered not open. Irvington Place runs down from Linden Avenue through a block of frame dwellings. The district is a residential neighbourhood of two and a half storey frame houses on narrow lots, with house numbers marked along each front, outbuildings behind them and several open lots. The principal institution is the group at the middle of Myrtle Avenue formed by St. Leo's Catholic Church, with the priest's house beside it, and, near Madison Avenue, St. Leo's Parochial School. Along Skinkle Lane are lumber storage sheds and the premises of J. Quinn, builder, and a wagon shed stands on Linden Avenue. A compass rose lies in the middle right and a scale of feet at the foot. The neighbouring sheet numbers 21 above, 27 on the left, 2 and 4 in the middle block corners, 30 below and 47 on the right are printed on the sheet, along with Library of Congress stamps. Water pipes, hydrants and a fire alarm box are marked in the streets.
notes: Cummings is Cummings Street and Bell, Stanley and Ruth are Bell Street, Stanley Street and Ruth Street in OpenStreetMap; Irvington Place and Skinkle Lane have no named way there today.
Linden Avenue / Madison Avenue and Cummings / Madison Avenue were not detected on the sheet.
Washington Avenue is drawn about 40 feet wide, narrower than the 50 feet of the modern right of way.
Only five junctions could be measured, so the fit rests on a few points; the fitted scale is 7.57 px/ft and the rotation 58.5 degrees.
50 ft. Cummings to Washington, Bell to Madison; St Leo church and school. 5 points.

sheet-29.description: Sheet 29 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows a residential part of Irvington on the north side of Springfield Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that the cross streets run across the page. Clinton Avenue forms the left edge, with Washington Avenue, Sharon Avenue, Bruen Avenue, Maple Avenue and South Grove running from it to the right, and Springfield Avenue crossing the upper right on a diagonal. The blocks between Sharon and South Grove are long, narrow lots with a regular row of frame dwellings, some stores and sheds fronting each street. At the upper left, between Washington and Sharon Avenues, the lots are mostly vacant, with a few dwellings and a training stable. A wedge of lots lies between Springfield Avenue and the end of Sharon Avenue, with the Speedway Tavern (stucco covered) at its point and a horse shed. East Speedway Avenue and the Essex County Speedway entrance appear at the right edge, and the upper right corner shows the start of Washington Avenue again on the far side of Springfield Avenue. Along Clinton Avenue stand an auto house, a small factory and several dwellings. The left margin carries the ends of Augusta, Howard, Grace and Maple streets from the neighbouring sheets, and block numbers 1 to 6 are printed in the blocks. Adjoining sheets are 31 and 32 on the left, 27 above, 30 on the right and 42 below.
notes: Clinton Avenue, Sharon Avenue, Bruen Avenue and Maple Avenue keep their names in OpenStreetMap; South Grove is Grove Street.
East Speedway Avenue is probably Eastern Parkway today (Eastern Parkway meets Sharon and Springfield Avenues at the same junction); this is an inference, not printed.
Washington Avenue at the top has been cut and realigned by the Garden State Parkway; it was not used for control.
50 ft. Washington, Sharon, Bruen, Maple Avs, South Grove, Clinton Av; 4 points along Clinton plus 1 hand pick (low).

sheet-30.description: Sheet 30 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the open land east of Springfield Avenue in Irvington, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. A band of lots fronts Washington Avenue along the top, ending at Madison Avenue at the upper right, where the compass rose is printed. Below it lies the Essex County Speedway, a long strip drawn as an open track with East Speedway Avenue running across the sheet, and a large blank tract below with a few scattered dwellings and sheds, one with a small coloured outbuilding. Springfield Avenue crosses the sheet on a broad diagonal, 85 feet wide, from the upper left to the lower right. On its southwest side lie the blocks between Bruen Avenue and Maple Avenue, with rows of dwellings on narrow lots, and the blocks between Maple Avenue and South Grove, which hold more dwellings and, near Springfield Avenue, a lumber yard (David Niebuhr, new and second hand lumber, with lumber piles and sheds), a garage, an electric motor shop and a cement block factory. North Grove Street continues the line of South Grove across Springfield Avenue at the bottom right. Brookside Avenue is lettered at the top right corner, and Alpine Avenue at the bottom left. Adjoining sheets are 28 above, 29 on the left, 47 on the right and 45 below.
notes: South Grove and North Grove Street are Grove Street in OpenStreetMap.
East Speedway Avenue is probably Eastern Parkway today; this is an inference, not printed.
Bruen Avenue / Springfield Avenue and Maple Avenue / Springfield Avenue were hand-picked from the drawn street edges.
50 ft. Washington, Madison, E. Speedway, Springfield, Bruen, Maple Avs; 2 hand picks (medium).

sheet-31.description: Sheet 31 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the centre of Irvington at the junction of Springfield, Clinton and Washington Avenues, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Springfield Avenue enters from the upper right and meets Clinton Avenue, which runs across the middle of the sheet. Union Avenue forms the left edge, Washington Avenue and Ball run down the right of the centre and Augusta is the right-hand cross street, with Cottage along the bottom. In the angle between Springfield and Clinton Avenues are the First Christian Church, a bank and lodge rooms, offices of a public service company and a moving picture theatre. South of Clinton Avenue stands the Brandenburgh Wagon Works, a large blue-coloured works for wagon manufacturing and auto repairing, with its forging shop, finishing floors and garage, beside Masonic Hall, a department store, hardware and paint shops, and a lumber yard (Stone-Post Co., builders supplies) with lumber sheds. A row of stores with dwellings fills the corner of Union and Clinton Avenues. East of Ball are dwellings on long lots, with a small brook crossing the lower right to Cottage. The top left holds the compass rose, with Myrtle Avenue and Skinkle Lane, and Sharon Avenue is lettered at the right edge. Adjoining sheets are 27 and 29 above and right, 12 on the left, 32 on the right and 34 below.
notes: Cottage is Nye Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Ball Street, Washington Avenue and Clinton Avenue meet at one node in OpenStreetMap, but the sheet draws Ball and Washington Avenue about 70 feet apart along Clinton Avenue; that node was not used.
The modern Springfield Avenue line did not agree with the drawn street here and Springfield Avenue was left out of the fit.
50 ft. Springfield, Washington, Clinton, Union Avs, Cottage (Nye Av), Ball, Augusta; 1 hand pick (low-medium).

sheet-32.description: Sheet 32 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows a residential district of Irvington between Cottage on the left and Clinton Avenue on the right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Augusta, Howard, Grace, Maple Avenue and South Grove run across the page from top to bottom, dividing the sheet into five long blocks. The lots are long and narrow, with the houses standing close to the street fronts. Along Augusta and Howard the lots near Clinton Avenue carry a row of two and three storey dwellings and a store, with a small number of dwellings and some outbuildings behind. Between Howard and Grace the frame dwellings are spread across the block, and a pink-coloured pair of dwellings stands on Grace near the centre. South of Grace an electrical supplies shop (F. W. Barb) stands on the next block, with dwellings along Maple Avenue. The last block between Maple Avenue and South Grove is mostly vacant, with a few dwellings drawn as built from plans and a stucco covered house. The compass rose is printed at the right, with Sharon Avenue, Bruen Avenue and Maple Avenue lettered across Clinton Avenue where they continue on sheet 29. Adjoining sheets are 31 above, 34 and 40 on the left, 29 on the right and 42 below.
notes: Cottage is Nye Avenue in OpenStreetMap; South Grove is Grove Street.
Clinton Avenue curves in the modern street network; its junctions here carry residuals of up to 3 m.
50 ft. Augusta, Howard, Grace, Maple Av, South Grove, Cottage, Clinton Av.

sheet-33.description: Sheet 33 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers undeveloped land in the southwest of Irvington, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Union Avenue runs along the top and Lyons Avenue, 80 feet wide, runs down the left edge, with Augusta crossing the lower part of the sheet from left to right. The area between Union Avenue and Augusta is mostly open ground, laid out in large tracts, with a small group of dwellings and sheds at the upper left beside Union Avenue and another dwelling and outbuildings near Lyons Avenue. A brook enters from the left edge and winds across the sheet toward the right, flowing northeast of the tracts and leaving by the right edge. A rank of narrow lots fronts Union Avenue at the upper right, with dwellings numbered from 96 to 140. Below Augusta lies a large pond, drawn in blue, filling a tract in the lower centre, with open land on either side. May is lettered as not opened at the lower right, and Howard Street appears at the right edge next to the lower right corner. Clermont Avenue is lettered at the left edge from the next sheet. The compass rose is at the right. Adjoining sheets are 10 above, 34 to the right, 35 on the left and 40 below.
notes: May is lettered "not opened" on the sheet; it exists today as May Street.
Only three junctions are measured on this sheet; the fit has no check against other points.
50 ft. Union and Lyons Avs, Clermont, Augusta, May, Howard; exact 3-point fit (low).

sheet-34.description: Sheet 34 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers a strip of southwest Irvington between Union Avenue at the top and Howard at the bottom, with May at the left and Cottage along the right edge, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. A single run of long lots fronts Union Avenue, most carrying a dwelling on the street with outbuildings and hen houses behind, and larger buildings of J. Howlett and Co., manufacturers of lead car seals, with a long narrow shop (used for wire pulling by Howlett and Co.) stretching from the factory toward the brook. A brook crosses the sheet from the left to the right edge, near the lettering of Ball, which is marked as not opened, and near a small group of buildings including two green-coloured shops. South of Ball lie further lots with dwellings, the larger ones on Augusta. Below Augusta is a block of narrow lots on Howard with dwellings, the left part being vacant lots running to May, which is also marked as not opened. The compass rose is at the upper left and Park Avenue is lettered at the upper right corner. Adjoining sheets are 10 and 12 above, 33 on the left, 31 and 32 on the right and 40 below.
notes: Cottage is Nye Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Ball and May are lettered "not opened" on the sheet; both exist today as Ball Street and May Street.
The drawn Ball and Union Avenue junctions with Cottage were not detected and are not used.
50 ft. Union and Park Avs, Cottage, Ball, Augusta, May, Howard; 4 points.

sheet-35.description: Sheet 35 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the north-west part of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Union Avenue runs down the whole left edge, on the north-west side of a large block of open land. Lyons Avenue crosses the top, with Clermont, Medbourne and Chester avenues running south from it and Welland Avenue and Fern Avenue crossing them. Between Lyons and Fern avenues the blocks are laid out in narrow lots, with scattered frame dwellings, outbuildings and a few stores. At the head of Chester Avenue stand the Lyons Avenue School and the Hose Company No. 1 house, both noted as heated by stove and lit by electricity, with a fire alarm box. Mount Vernon Avenue runs south-east from Clermont Avenue past Irvington Public School No. 5, a large blue-shaded concrete building noted as built from plans, and bends towards Prospect Avenue. In the lower right, Berkshire Place and Melville Place are crossed by Mount Vernon Avenue in a small platted block of frame dwellings, with Rosehill Place leading off to the north-east. Prospect Avenue runs diagonally across the bottom right, and in the bottom left a row of long glass and hot houses stands near Union Avenue. Large parts of the sheet, on the west side of Clermont Avenue, are unsubdivided farm and garden land with only a few buildings. A compass rose and the scale bar are printed on the right and bottom. Adjoining sheets are 33 above, 39 and 38 to the east, 37 below right and 36 and 6 and 7 on the west and south.
notes: Clermont Avenue is Cleremont Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Prospect Avenue is Chancellor Avenue today.
The Garden State Parkway and Union Avenue modern alignments cut across the open land on the west side; Union Avenue was not used as control.
Mt. is printed in Mt. Vernon; written out as Mount in the street list.
100 ft. Lyons Av to Prospect Av (Chancellor Av), Union Av to Chester Av; Union Av and Berkshire Pl left out.

sheet-36.description: Sheet 36 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers a strip of farmland in the south-west corner of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Union Avenue runs down the left side of the sheet from Prospect Avenue at the top, nearly straight for most of its length and then bending south-west towards the lower left corner, where it meets Elizabeth Road at the Union County line. Prospect Avenue appears only as a short east-west stub at the top, bending north-east at its right end. A lane with no other name leaves Union Avenue near the middle and runs east to a property line. The rest of the sheet is large irregular lots of open land with a handful of frame buildings: a farmhouse and outbuildings near the top, a chicken farm with coops and a cleaning house beside Union Avenue, and a few more dwellings and a coop lower down. The Union County line crosses the sheet diagonally from lower left to right, marked by a dash-dot line and lettered. Small buildings near the bottom left stand around the bend of Union Avenue and Elizabeth Road. Street widths are lettered as 50, 45 and 40 feet. A compass rose is printed at the upper left, the scale bar and a Library of Congress stamp at the bottom. Adjoining sheets are 35 above, 37 to the east, and 5 and 6 on the west.
notes: Prospect Avenue is Chancellor Avenue today.
Elizabeth Road is not a named way in OpenStreetMap; the junction with Union Avenue is taken as the modern Mill Road and Union Avenue node (low confidence).
The lane is lettered only as Lane.
100 ft. Union Av farmland to the county line; anchored on one hand pick (low).

sheet-37.description: Sheet 37 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the southern edge of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and mostly open farmland. Prospect Avenue crosses the top from the left edge up to the right, 45 feet wide, with Mount Vernon Avenue entering from the north at a fire alarm box and Chestnut Avenue leaving to the south-east a short way beyond. Further east Norwood Avenue and Coit Street enter Prospect Avenue from the north. Chestnut Avenue runs the full height of the sheet, 50 feet wide, bending once near the middle, and carries the few buildings of the sheet: a group of farm buildings with coops on its west side, and a small cluster near the Union County line at the lower right. The Union County line crosses the lower part of the sheet as a lettered dash-dot line. A house with outbuildings stands at the top between Prospect and Chestnut avenues. Other buildings are scattered, and most of the ground is large lots outlined by property lines without buildings. A compass rose with a griffin north pointer is printed in the upper right, turned about 25 degrees from vertical, and the scale bar and Library of Congress stamp are at the bottom. Adjoining sheets are 35 on the left, 36 below left, 38 on the right and 39 above right.
notes: Prospect Avenue is Chancellor Avenue today and is drawn 45 feet wide.
Only the junctions along Prospect Avenue are used as control, so the placement rests on four points along one line.
100 ft. Prospect Av (Chancellor Av) with Mt Vernon, Chestnut, Norwood, Coit; 4 points on one line (low); second pass moved it 27.6 m at the far corner (shared junctions 3.7 to 1.6 m).

sheet-38.description: Sheet 38 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the south-east side of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. In the upper left two blocks of narrow lots between Mount Vernon Avenue and Norwood Avenue are divided by Berkshire Place and Melville Place and hold frame dwellings, outbuildings and coops. Prospect Avenue runs east below them and then south-east across the sheet, with Chestnut Avenue leaving it near the left edge and running south to the Union County line. East of Norwood Avenue a second platted area with a street called Court runs north-east, and Woolsey Street and Cordier Street come in from the north-east. Near the centre of the sheet are C. C. Lienau's Sons Co., structural iron works, and the Lehigh Valley Railroad, which curves up from the lower left past them; to the south-east, between Prospect Avenue and the city line, is a nursery with a long group of hot houses and glass roofs. Large areas elsewhere are blank lots outlined by property lines. A compass rose is printed at the upper right and the Union County line and the line of the Town of Irvington cross the lower part. Adjoining sheets are 35 and 39 above, 37 on the left and 51 below.
notes: Prospect Avenue is Chancellor Avenue today.
The street printed Court has no modern name in OpenStreetMap and was not used as control.
The Lehigh Valley Railroad line is lettered L. V. R. R.
100 ft. Berkshire / Melville Pl, Prospect Av to Cordier St.

sheet-39.description: Sheet 39 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the central south of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that Lyons Avenue and the cross streets run up and down the page. Chester Avenue crosses the top, with Fern Avenue, Welland Avenue and Lyons Avenue running south from it, crossed by Normandy Place and then by Coit. The blocks between Fern Avenue and Lyons Avenue are narrow residential lots with frame dwellings, many of them on large lots, and a few stores along Lyons Avenue; a fire alarm box stands at the corner of Lyons Avenue and Coit. In the upper left Mount Vernon Avenue, Berkshire Place, Norwood Avenue, Rose Hill Place and Melville Place cross each other diagonally in a platted block of small frame houses, and the Union Trowel Works stands at the south end of Fern Avenue. Below Coit, large blocks are lettered Woolsey and Cordier; the Lehigh Valley Railroad crosses the lower part, with the Surges Concrete Block Co., J. Reitzel and Co. pickle products, the Empire Sash, Blind and Door Co. and a hot-house nursery beside it. Prospect Avenue runs down the left edge. The Town of Irvington city line crosses the bottom. A compass rose is at the left. Adjoining sheets are 35 and 38 on the left and 40 and 41 on the right and 51 below.
notes: Prospect Avenue is Chancellor Avenue today; its junctions here are 2 to 4 m off the modern line and were left out of the fit.
Rose Hill Place is Rosehill Place in OpenStreetMap; Coit, Woolsey and Cordier are Coit Street, Woolsey Street and Cordier Street.
South Grove Street is printed S. Grove St. at the right edge; the modern Grove Street runs on a different line.
100 ft, turned. Chester Av to Cordier St, Fern, Welland, Lyons Avs; Chancellor Av left out (widened).

sheet-40.description: Sheet 40 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers the central part of the Town of Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. In the upper left Howard, Grace and Maple Avenue run south from Cottage to May, with the long blocks between them cut into very narrow lots that are almost wholly vacant apart from a few dwellings on Grace and Maple. East of May, South Grove and Coit run south to Lyons Avenue, and the blocks between Coit and Woolsey and east of Woolsey hold a line of factories: Atlas Metal Mfg. Co. and Jennings Silver Co., Eastern Cut Sole Co., Jos. Ross Jr. and Co., the Irvington Mfg. Co., the Anderson Mfg. Co., Wickens and Dickinson, Richard Best, and the Gloriete Smelting and Refining Works. The L. V. R. R. switch runs south along Woolsey Street and a branch curves off to the lower right. Large blank areas to the lower left are marked Essex County Park Commission. Lyons Avenue runs diagonally across the bottom, with Chester Avenue, Normandy Place, Coit Street and Woolsey Street crossing it. A compass rose, scale bar and Library of Congress stamp are at the bottom, and the right edge carries a stub of 21st Street. Adjoining sheets are 32, 42 and 34 above, 33 and 39 below and 41 on the right.
notes: Cottage is Nye Avenue today; Howard, Grace, May, Coit and Woolsey are Howard Street, Grace Street, May Street, Coit Street and Woolsey Street.
South Grove is printed S. Grove and is Grove Street today.
The detector used the Irvington Industrial Track crossing at Lyons Avenue as one point.
100 ft. Howard to Woolsey, Cottage to Lyons Av; factories (repeats sheet 13), Essex County Park Commission land.

sheet-41.description: Sheet 41 of the 1909 Newark volume five covers a strip of the Newark and Irvington boundary country, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that the streets run slantwise across the page. Nye Avenue and its western continuation Cottage cross the top; Lyons Avenue crosses the bottom on a long diagonal. Between them, on the right of the sheet, run Fabyan Place, Schley Street and Wainwright Street, crossed by Bragaw Avenue and Shaw Avenue, with the numbered blocks 3071 to 3090. The east side is a mixed district of small frame dwellings on narrow lots, some on lots still empty. The main industrial use lies in the middle: the J. S. Hobbs lumber yard at the head of Glorieux Street, the American Coal Chute Co. iron works on Buffington Street, the J. T. Castles Ice Cream Co. with its mixing and freezing rooms, wagon shed and engine room on Loretto Street, and the Brown and Rusling Co. cut and sawed stone plant, then in course of construction, off Shaw Avenue. The Lehigh Valley Railroad runs down the left side in several tracks with a curved siding to the stone plant. The Town of Irvington and City of Newark boundary is lettered along the middle of the sheet. A compass rose shows north to the upper left. The left third of the sheet is blank, the territory of adjoining sheets 13, 39 and 40, and sheets 42, 51 and 54 lie on the other sides.
notes: Cottage, the street at the top left, is the west part of modern Nye Avenue.
Saranac Place is not in OpenStreetMap today.
The Town of Irvington and City line is lettered across the middle of the sheet.
Names were read from the overview at reduced size, not on 1:1 crops (medium confidence).
100 ft. Nye Av, Cottage, Glorieux, Saranac, Birks, Fabyan Pls, Schley, Wainwright, Lyons Av; L.V.R.R.

sheet-42.description: Sheet 42 of the 1909 Newark volume five shows the district where South Grove Street, Coit Street and Clinton Avenue meet, on the boundary of Newark and Irvington, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 58 degrees so that Clinton Avenue runs diagonally down the middle of the page. At the top are South Grove Street and Harrison Place with blocks of narrow lots and scattered frame dwellings, and Coit Street, with the Coit Street Public School. Along the west side runs Cottage, today the west part of Nye Avenue, with Woolsey Street crossing it. The middle left is industrial: the Lehigh Valley Railroad yard with several tracks, the L. V. R.R. freight station, the Lehigh Valley Coal Co. coal chutes, N. Drake coal yard, mill and elevator, John Wittel artificial stone company, Standard Building Block Co. cement block works, Cook and Genung Co. masons' supplies and Tomkins Bros. At the bottom are Saranac, Birks, Fabyan Places, Hawthorne Avenue, Voorhees Street and Beverly Street, with rows of frame houses and the Town of Irvington City line lettered diagonally. To the right are 22nd, 21st and Montgomery Streets with Alpine Avenue at the edge. A compass rose at the upper left shows north to the upper right. Blocks are numbered 1 to 7 at the top and 3079 to 3091 at the bottom.
notes: South Grove is modern Grove Street.
Cottage is the west part of modern Nye Avenue.
Alpine Avenue and Saranac Place are not in OpenStreetMap today.
21st Street at Nye Avenue was rejected by the fit as 18.6 m from the modern node.
